overview:
Gommatasara Karma-kanda is one of the most important technical treatises on karma in the Digambara Jain tradition, composed by Acharya Nemichandra Siddhanta Chakravarti (c. 10th–11th century CE). It forms the second half of the larger work Gommatasara, whose first part, Jiva-kanda, analyzes the nature, classifications, and spiritual progress of the soul (jiva), while Karma-kanda focuses on the non-soul side of reality—specifically, the subtle material karmic aggregates that bind the soul in saṃsāra. Together, the two parts expand and systematize the concise doctrinal outline of Nemichandra’s Dravya-saṃgraha, which begins from the distinction between living and non-living substances and then proceeds to the seven tattvas and the path of liberation.

Karma-kanda is a highly structured, verse-based text (traditionally counted as 972 gāthās) that offers a meticulous taxonomy of karmic matter (pudgala) and its interaction with the soul. It explains the nature (svabhāva) of karma, the modes of bondage (bandha), operation (udaya), and subsistence (sthiti), and the complex numerical classifications of karmic types and subtypes. The work distinguishes eight primary categories of karma—knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇīya), perception-obscuring (darśanāvaraṇīya), deluding (mohanīya), obstructive (antarāya), feeling-producing (vedanīya), body-making (nāma), status-determining (gotra), and lifespan-determining (āyu)—and then further subdivides them into numerous prakṛtis and sub-prakṛtis. These classifications are not merely theoretical; they are meant to show how specific mental states, passions (kaṣāya), and activities (yoga) generate particular karmic bonds and thus particular experiences and embodiments.

The text is organized into multiple chapters or sections (often called adhikāras or chūlikās) that move from definition to application. Early portions describe the nature of karmic atoms, their quantitative measures, and their relation to the five kinds of bodies (śarīra). Subsequent sections treat the causes of inflow (āśrava) and bondage, the rules governing the duration (sthiti) and intensity (anubhāga) of karmas, and the ways in which karmas are distributed across different spiritual stages (guṇasthāna) and soul-quests (mārgana). Later chapters discuss special thought-activities, the triad of time (past, present, future) in relation to karmic existence, and the methods of classifying karmas according to their duration and fruition. The final verses traditionally include a brief account of the composition and transmission of the text itself.

Philosophically, Gommatasara Karma-kanda stands at the intersection of metaphysics, ethics, and soteriology. Metaphysically, it presupposes the Jain doctrine of six substances (dravyas)—jiva, pudgala, dharma, adharma, kāla, and ākāśa—and treats karma as a specific form of pudgala that can be measured, classified, and analyzed without reducing it to mere metaphor. Ethically, it links karmic bondage to concrete states of mind and conduct, showing how passions, negligence, and wrong belief intensify bondage, while restraint, right faith, and disciplined practice lead to the stoppage (saṃvara) and shedding (nirjarā) of karmas. Soteriologically, it maps karmic processes onto the fourteen guṇasthānas, demonstrating how the gradual purification of the soul corresponds to the progressive weakening and final destruction of karmic bonds.

In the broader history of Jain thought, Karma-kanda is a cornerstone of the Digambara siddhānta (doctrinal) literature. It synthesizes earlier canonical and post-canonical materials into a coherent, numerically precise system that became foundational for later commentaries and pedagogical texts. Modern editions and translations—such as the English translation by Rai Bahadur J. L. Jaini (1927) and the critical Sanskrit/Prakrit editions prepared under scholars like A. N. Upadhye and Kailash Chandra Shastri—have made the work accessible to contemporary students of Jainism. For advanced study of karma theory, gunasthānas, and the technical vocabulary of Jain metaphysics, Gommatasara Karma-kanda remains one of the primary reference texts, though its dense classifications are best approached alongside traditional commentaries and under the guidance of qualified teachers.

Because of its technical nature, the text is not intended as a stand-alone manual for lay practice or medical, psychological, or legal decision-making. Rather, it offers a conceptual map of karmic processes that can inform ethical reflection and spiritual discipline when interpreted within a living tradition. Questions about how its teachings apply to specific life situations—especially those involving health, mental well-being, family responsibilities, or vows with serious bodily consequences—should be discussed with experienced Jain scholars and spiritual guides who can integrate scriptural insight with practical wisdom.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasara Karma-kanda
primary_sources.author: Acharya Nemichandra Siddhanta Chakravarti
primary_sources.original_text:
गोमटसार (कमकाड)
मंगलाचरण एवं स्थितिः
श्री नमो अरिहंताणं, नमो सिद्धाणं, नमो आयरियाणं, नमो उवज्झायाणं, नमो लोए सव्वसाहूणं।
primary_sources.transliteration:
Gommaṭasāra (Karmakāṇḍa)
Maṅgalācaraṇa evaṃ sthitiḥ
Śrī namo arihantāṇaṃ, namo siddhāṇaṃ, namo āyariyāṇaṃ, namo uvajjhāyāṇaṃ, namo loe savvasāhūṇaṃ.
primary_sources.translation:
Gommatasara (Section on Karma)
Invocation and context:
Reverent salutation to the Arhats, salutation to the Siddhas, salutation to the Ācāryas, salutation to the Upādhyāyas, salutation to all the Sādhus in the world.
primary_sources.notes: This opening reflects the standard Jain pañca-namaskāra, situating Karma-kanda within the broader framework of Jain devotion and respect for the fourfold order and liberated beings. The text then proceeds to define the term ‘karma’, enumerate the eight principal karmas and their subtypes, and lay out the structure of the work in terms of gāthās and chapters. The surviving manuscripts and printed editions are in mixed Prakrit-Sanskrit, with Devanagari script commonly used in modern publications.

primary_sources.title: Dravya-saṃgraha (as doctrinal basis)
primary_sources.author: Acharya Nemichandra Siddhanta Chakravarti
primary_sources.original_text:
जिवाजिवं दव्वं, तत्तं तं च तत्त्वं।
संसारमोक्षमार्गो, तं चोवदइ णेमिचंद्रो॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
Jivājivaṃ davvaṃ, tattaṃ taṃ ca tattvaṃ.
Saṃsāramokṣamārgo, taṃ covadai Nemicaṃdro.
primary_sources.translation:
The living and the non-living are substances, and these are the principles (tattvas).
The path of saṃsāra and liberation—this Nemichandra expounds.
primary_sources.notes: Dravya-saṃgraha is a brief doctrinal poem that Nemichandra himself expands in Gommatasara Jiva-kanda and Karma-kanda. While not part of Karma-kanda proper, it provides the conceptual framework: the distinction between jiva and ajiva, the enumeration of tattvas, and the path to liberation. Karma-kanda can be read as a detailed exposition of the non-living karmic matter implied in these verses.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasara Karma-kanda (structure summary from traditional editions)
primary_sources.author: Acharya Nemichandra Siddhanta Chakravarti
primary_sources.original_text:
गोमटसार कमकाड विषय-सूची
भाग I: कम के पाठमक साथ कथन (गाथा 1–86)
भाग II: बंध, उदय और स्थिति के अधिकार (गाथा 87–357)
भाग III: विभिन्न अवस्थाओं का वर्णन (गाथा 358–397)
भाग IV: उप-अध्याय (गाथा 398–450)
भाग V–X: आश्रव, भाव, विशेष विचार, अवधि-विभाजन, तथा ग्रंथ-इतिहास (गाथा 451–972)।
primary_sources.transliteration:
Gommaṭasāra Karmakāṇḍa viṣaya-sūcī
Bhāga I: karma ke prāthamika sātha kathana (gāthā 1–86)
Bhāga II: bandha, udaya aura sthiti ke adhikāra (gāthā 87–357)
Bhāga III: vibhinn avasthāoṃ kā varṇana (gāthā 358–397)
Bhāga IV: up-adhyāya (gāthā 398–450)
Bhāga V–X: āśrava, bhāva, viśeṣa vicāra, avadhi-vibhājana, tathā grantha-itihāsa (gāthā 451–972).
primary_sources.translation:
Table of contents of Gommatasara Karma-kanda:
Part I: Fundamental exposition of karma (verses 1–86).
Part II: Chapters on bondage, fruition, and duration of karmas (verses 87–357).
Part III: Description of various states of karmic existence (verses 358–397).
Part IV: Sub-chapter elaborating the preceding topics (verses 398–450).
Parts V–X: Sections on inflow (āśrava), states of being (bhāva), special thought-activities, distribution of karmas by duration, and the history of the composition of the book (verses 451–972).
primary_sources.notes: This summary reflects the internal structure as preserved in modern critical editions. The exact headings and verse counts can vary slightly across manuscripts, but the overall ten-part division is widely accepted in Digambara scholastic tradition. It shows how the text moves from definition to application, and finally to meta-reflection on its own composition.

misconceptions.myth: Gommatasara Karma-kanda is only a ritual or devotional text and does not have philosophical significance.
misconceptions.reality: Karma-kanda is a highly technical doctrinal treatise that systematically analyzes the nature, classification, and operation of karmic matter. While it begins with a devotional invocation, the bulk of the text is devoted to precise metaphysical and ethical classifications that underpin Jain karma theory and the doctrine of guṇasthānas. It is central to Digambara philosophical literature, not merely a ritual manual.

misconceptions.myth: The detailed classifications of karma in Gommatasara Karma-kanda imply a rigid, fatalistic view of destiny that leaves no room for ethical effort.
misconceptions.reality: Although Karma-kanda offers very precise numerical and qualitative classifications of karmas, it repeatedly links karmic bondage to specific mental states, passions, and activities, and emphasizes the roles of right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct in stopping inflow (saṃvara) and shedding (nirjarā). The text presupposes that ethical discipline and spiritual practice can transform one’s karmic situation; its classifications are meant to clarify how effort works, not to deny its possibility.

misconceptions.myth: Because Gommatasara Karma-kanda is a core Digambara text, its teachings can be directly used to make medical, psychological, or legal decisions without further guidance.
misconceptions.reality: Karma-kanda is a doctrinal and metaphysical work, not a handbook for medical, mental-health, or legal decision-making. Its descriptions of karma, lifespan, and bodily states are framed within a spiritual context and require careful interpretation. Applying its teachings to concrete life situations—especially those involving health, mental well-being, family responsibilities, or vows with serious bodily consequences—should be done in consultation with qualified Jain teachers and appropriate professional experts, rather than on the basis of textual study alone.

misconceptions.myth: The text is relevant only for monks and nuns and has no value for lay practitioners or students of Jain philosophy.
misconceptions.reality: While Gommatasara Karma-kanda is indeed advanced and traditionally studied in monastic and scholastic settings, its conceptual framework—especially the analysis of karma, guṇasthānas, and ethical causality—has informed lay education and modern scholarship as well. With suitable guidance and supporting commentaries, serious lay students and academic researchers can engage with the text to deepen their understanding of Jain metaphysics and ethics, even if they do not adopt monastic disciplines.
